top_stories.title: Startups Are Picking Names That Can Work Even If The Original Business Model Doesn’t
top_stories.content: Startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor. For a few years, founders might be enamoured of silly monikers, made-up words, and creative misspellings. Then the pendulum swings, and startups defer to simple names that describe what they actually do. So where are we now? Probably somewhere in the middle. Per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague. It’s a preference that reflects this era of fast-evolving AI, in which founders want room to adapt. Examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups. There’s Also, which is of course a micromobility spin-out. Perplexity is a genAI company although you couldn’t tell that by its name. And then there’s Sunday, which makes household robots, in case that wasn’t clear from the name. “Reality is a lot of these companies, in seven or eight years they’ve done at least one or two major pivots,” Athol Foden, who runs the naming consultancy Brighter Naming, told us. That makes it logical to pick a name that can still work afterward. Running out of names When startups do make inventive picks, it’s often out of necessity rather than preference. “We’re running out of words. Everything is trademarked multiple times over,” said Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. “So we have to look for something unexpected. Given that reality, Benedini is always on the lookout for startups that exemplify the element of surprise. One standout is Hugging Face, the AI model sharing and development platform, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September. It didn’t succeed just because of its strange name, obviously, but it didn’t hurt. items.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
items.content: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook. Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history, ai, generative-ai, llms, a

items.title: AI Bias In HR: Why Polished Work Gets Overrated And What to Do About It
items.content: In today’s world, all professional employees use AI, whether it’s candidates submitting highly polished CVs with 100% perfect fit with your job description to AI-generated work. In this environment, how can we promote the right employees and how do we hire the best canidates when everyone appears to be perfect? Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo. It reads beautifully and recommends buying a company at what looks like a reasonable price. There’s one problem. The model counted the same revenue twice. One candidate improves the slides. The other asks for the source data, spots the error and changes the recommendation. If I’d asked for a polished take-home assignment and used AI to grade it, I might have hired the better slide editor. AI has become a significant part of how people apply for jobs and how they do that work. Using AI to police that behavior is a losing game. Employers have more to gain by making AI use visible and designing hiring and performance reviews around what people do with it. The better AI gets at writing résumés, the less a perfect match tells you Indeed illustrates both sides of the hiring loop. Its Career Scout offers job seekers résumé help, while its employer tools help review applications against hiring criteria. Both can save time, and résumé assistance can help a qualified applicant explain experience they’ve struggled to put into words. But it can also make two very different candidates look equally well-suited for a role on paper. An AI detector adds another score without answering the question the employer cares about: Could this person do the job? I’d use AI to help the recruiter prepare a better follow-up. If someone says they led an integration, ask them to walk through a decision they made when two teams disagreed. The résumé gets you to the question. The answer gives you something to evaluate. items.title: How Daniel Zeltser cold-emailed his way to employee #2 at Beacon Health
items.content: Daniel Zeltser was a student at Duke University when he cold-emailed the CEO of a tiny healthcare startup. Then he followed up. Then he followed up again — enough times that Mark, the CEO, finally answered. "He said he had ten minutes for a call; we talked for thirty." They agreed on a two-week trial. About a week in, Obinna, the CTO, told him he was staying. "So apparently my first contribution was being very difficult to ignore."That startup was Beacon Health (W26), a YC startup that builds AI agents to take repetitive work off medical teams' plates — sorting incoming documents, updating patient records, and making sure care doesn't fall through the cracks. Daniel joined as employee #2.Why he took the leapWhat pulled Daniel away from school wasn't a pitch deck. It was the people and the problem. "The idea that something I built could help a medical team take better care of its patients was pretty hard to pass up," he says. "I wanted to find out what I could do with that kind of responsibility."He evaluated Beacon Health the way you'd evaluate a team, not a company. During his trial, he watched how the founders treated each other, how seriously they took the practices they worked with, and how much they enjoyed the problem. "That told me a lot more than a pitch could."What he actually buildsDaniel owns the full product engineering loop: get on a call with a medical practice, understand what's eating up their day, build the workflow, and make sure it works for them. His title is founding engineer, but he'd call the real job "whatever gets us unstuck today."He built a workflow that checks patient charts against a care-gap portal, finds care that's already happened but hasn't been recorded, and updates it with supporting evidence — so practices get credit, and get paid, for keeping patients healthy. items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.content: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. items.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
items.content: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. all_items.title: Startups Are Picking Names That Can Work Even If The Original Business Model Doesn’t
all_items.content: Startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor. For a few years, founders might be enamoured of silly monikers, made-up words, and creative misspellings. Then the pendulum swings, and startups defer to simple names that describe what they actually do. So where are we now? Probably somewhere in the middle. Per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague. It’s a preference that reflects this era of fast-evolving AI, in which founders want room to adapt. Examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups. There’s Also, which is of course a micromobility spin-out. Perplexity is a genAI company although you couldn’t tell that by its name. And then there’s Sunday, which makes household robots, in case that wasn’t clear from the name. “Reality is a lot of these companies, in seven or eight years they’ve done at least one or two major pivots,” Athol Foden, who runs the naming consultancy Brighter Naming, told us. That makes it logical to pick a name that can still work afterward. Running out of names When startups do make inventive picks, it’s often out of necessity rather than preference. “We’re running out of words. Everything is trademarked multiple times over,” said Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. “So we have to look for something unexpected. Given that reality, Benedini is always on the lookout for startups that exemplify the element of surprise. One standout is Hugging Face, the AI model sharing and development platform, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September. It didn’t succeed just because of its strange name, obviously, but it didn’t hurt. all_items.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
all_items.content: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook. Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history, ai, generative-ai, llms, a

all_items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
all_items.content: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. all_items.title: AI Bias In HR: Why Polished Work Gets Overrated And What to Do About It
all_items.content: In today’s world, all professional employees use AI, whether it’s candidates submitting highly polished CVs with 100% perfect fit with your job description to AI-generated work. In this environment, how can we promote the right employees and how do we hire the best canidates when everyone appears to be perfect? Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo. It reads beautifully and recommends buying a company at what looks like a reasonable price. There’s one problem. The model counted the same revenue twice. One candidate improves the slides. The other asks for the source data, spots the error and changes the recommendation. If I’d asked for a polished take-home assignment and used AI to grade it, I might have hired the better slide editor. AI has become a significant part of how people apply for jobs and how they do that work. Using AI to police that behavior is a losing game. Employers have more to gain by making AI use visible and designing hiring and performance reviews around what people do with it. The better AI gets at writing résumés, the less a perfect match tells you Indeed illustrates both sides of the hiring loop. Its Career Scout offers job seekers résumé help, while its employer tools help review applications against hiring criteria. Both can save time, and résumé assistance can help a qualified applicant explain experience they’ve struggled to put into words. But it can also make two very different candidates look equally well-suited for a role on paper. An AI detector adds another score without answering the question the employer cares about: Could this person do the job? I’d use AI to help the recruiter prepare a better follow-up. If someone says they led an integration, ask them to walk through a decision they made when two teams disagreed. The résumé gets you to the question. The answer gives you something to evaluate. all_items.title: How Daniel Zeltser cold-emailed his way to employee #2 at Beacon Health
all_items.content: Daniel Zeltser was a student at Duke University when he cold-emailed the CEO of a tiny healthcare startup. Then he followed up. Then he followed up again — enough times that Mark, the CEO, finally answered. "He said he had ten minutes for a call; we talked for thirty." They agreed on a two-week trial. About a week in, Obinna, the CTO, told him he was staying. "So apparently my first contribution was being very difficult to ignore."That startup was Beacon Health (W26), a YC startup that builds AI agents to take repetitive work off medical teams' plates — sorting incoming documents, updating patient records, and making sure care doesn't fall through the cracks. Daniel joined as employee #2.Why he took the leapWhat pulled Daniel away from school wasn't a pitch deck. It was the people and the problem. "The idea that something I built could help a medical team take better care of its patients was pretty hard to pass up," he says. "I wanted to find out what I could do with that kind of responsibility."He evaluated Beacon Health the way you'd evaluate a team, not a company. During his trial, he watched how the founders treated each other, how seriously they took the practices they worked with, and how much they enjoyed the problem. "That told me a lot more than a pitch could."What he actually buildsDaniel owns the full product engineering loop: get on a call with a medical practice, understand what's eating up their day, build the workflow, and make sure it works for them. His title is founding engineer, but he'd call the real job "whatever gets us unstuck today."He built a workflow that checks patient charts against a care-gap portal, finds care that's already happened but hasn't been recorded, and updates it with supporting evidence — so practices get credit, and get paid, for keeping patients healthy.
